title: Multi-AZ
subtitle: Intra-region fault domain isolation, synchronous storage replication, and cross-AZ network cost optimization.
keyTakeaways: An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more discrete data centers with independent power, cooling, and physical networking within a metropolitan region, connected by low-latency (<2ms) dark fiber.
Low inter-AZ latency (0.5ms - 2ms) enables synchronous database replication and consensus quorums (Raft/Paxos) across 3 AZs with zero data loss (RPO = 0) on single-AZ failure.
Cross-AZ data transfer is billed by cloud providers ($0.01-$0.02/GB each way); high-throughput systems use Topology-Aware Routing to keep RPC and cache reads within the local AZ.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Multi-AZ is a foundational architectural concept in distributed systems. Intra-region fault domain isolation, synchronous storage replication, and cross-AZ network cost optimization. Fundamentally, A single data center can fail due to transformer explosions, cooling leaks, or fiber cuts. Cloud regions group 3 or more physically separated Availability Zones (typically 10-100 km apart) so they do not share Flood/Power fault domains, while keeping round-trip network latency under 2 milliseconds.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more discrete data centers with independent power, cooling, and physical networking within a metropolitan region, connected by low-latency (<2ms) dark fiber.

**Problem Space & Invariants**: Low inter-AZ latency (0.5ms - 2ms) enables synchronous database replication and consensus quorums (Raft/Paxos) across 3 AZs with zero data loss (RPO = 0) on single-AZ failure.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: In production distributed systems, multi-az manifests across several distinct architectural classifications, operational modes, and implementation strategies:
bullets: **Cross-AZ Load Balancing (Uniform Distribution)**: Focuses on evenly balances cpu/memory across all instances regardless of uneven ingress distribution per az. Best suited for Low-bandwidth, CPU-intensive RPC services where even compute utilization outweighs network transfer fees..

**Zonal Affinity / Topology-Aware Routing**: Focuses on eliminates cross-az network egress charges and shaves 1-2ms per hop across deep microservice chains. Best suited for High-bandwidth data pipelines, Kafka consumers, distributed caches, and chatty microservice meshes..

Why 3 AZs Instead of 2: Consensus protocols (etcd, Raft, ZooKeeper, Patroni) require a strict majority quorum ($\lfloor N/2 \rfloor + 1$). With 2 AZs, a majority is $\lfloor 2/2 \rfloor + 1 = 2$—meaning if either AZ goes dark, the cluster loses quorum and halts writes! With 3 AZs, quorum is 2, surviving any single AZ loss.

Synchronous Storage Durability: Cloud-native databases (AWS Aurora, CockroachDB) write WAL logs across 6 storage nodes spanning 3 AZs and acknowledge commits once 4 of 6 nodes confirm, achieving RPO = 0 with ~1.5ms write overhead.

Topology-Aware Service Routing: Configure Envoy / Kubernetes EndpointSlices to route RPCs to healthy pods in the same AZ first, spilling over to peer AZs only when local capacity is saturated or unhealthy.

Kafka Rack-Aware Consumers: Set `client.rack` on consumers and `broker.rack` on Kafka brokers so consumers fetch high-volume partition replicas from the local AZ's follower broker rather than crossing AZs to the leader.

codeSnippet.title: Kubernetes Topology Spread Constraints & Zone-Aware Routing
codeSnippet.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payment-service
spec:
  replicas: 6
  template:
    spec:
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: payment-service
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payment-service
  annotations:
    # Prefer routing traffic to pods within the caller's same AZ
    service.kubernetes.io/topology-mode: Auto

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Adopting appropriate design patterns around multi-az unlocks critical performance, scalability, and operational advantages for modern backend platforms:
bullets: **Where to Use — High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Low-bandwidth, CPU-intensive RPC services where even compute utilization outweighs network transfer fees. and environments requiring Evenly balances CPU/memory across all instances regardless of uneven ingress distribution per AZ..

**Where to Use — High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for High-bandwidth data pipelines, Kafka consumers, distributed caches, and chatty microservice meshes. where Eliminates cross-AZ network egress charges and shaves 1-2ms per hop across deep microservice chains..

**How to Use — Engineering Implementation**: While Multi-AZ protects against data center failures, naive round-robin load balancing across 3 AZs means 66% of every microservice hop, Redis read, and Kafka consumer fetch crosses an AZ boundary—incurring bilateral data transfer charges and adding 1-2ms per hop.. Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: While essential for scalable engineering, multi-az introduces substantial architectural trade-offs, operational failure modes, and anti-patterns if applied inappropriately:
bullets: **Where to Avoid — Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints impose 66% of traffic crosses az boundaries, incurring $0.02/gb transfer fees and extra 1ms latency per hop.
**Where to Avoid — Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid premature optimization when can cause hot-spotting if one az has fewer healthy pods or receives disproportionate ingress traffic.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Mastering multi-az is a defining trait of Staff-level distributed systems engineers. Navigating the delicate balance between performance, reliability, and simplicity ensures architectures scale sustainably without introducing unmanageable operational friction.
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Cross-AZ data transfer is billed by cloud providers ($0.01-$0.02/GB each way); high-throughput systems use Topology-Aware Routing to keep RPC and cache reads within the local AZ.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Always explain why production stateful systems deploy across **3 AZs** rather than 2: in a 2-AZ setup, if the AZ hosting the primary (or 50% of quorum nodes) loses connectivity, the surviving AZ only has 50% of votes and cannot safely elect a new leader without risking split-brain.
